agentCan: Fill the console forms (APIs, scopes, callback URL) given account access
Implement the full 3LO flow including accessible-resources/cloudid discovery and rotating refresh-token persistence
Draft the Marketplace third-party-integration listing packet

approval.cost: No fee mentioned in the docs reviewed (unstated)
approval.trigger: No review to build or share: enable sharing in the console and any user can authorize immediately. The catch is cosmetic but real: users of an unapproved integration are warned it 'has not yet been reviewed by Atlassian'. Removing the warning requires the Atlassian Marketplace third-party-integration approval (an informational listing; a reviewer tests your software and needs access to a test instance).
approval.wait: General Marketplace listing guidance states you should hear from a support member within 5-10 business days (not a 3LO-specific SLA)

blockers.detail: Unless offline_access is in the authorize request's scope, you get no refresh token and users redo the whole flow when the access token expires. With it, refresh tokens rotate: every use returns a new pair and disables the old one, with a 90-day inactivity expiry. Failing to persist the newest token is a documented invalid_grant cause; a user's password change also invalidates refresh tokens.
blockers.howToClear: Always request offline_access for agents, and store the replacement refresh token on every single refresh.
blockers.title: No refresh token without offline_access

blockers.detail: API calls are per-site: api.atlassian.com/ex/jira/{cloudid}/..., and you must discover sites via the accessible-resources endpoint first. With resource-level grants, tokens work only for the site(s) the user picked on the consent screen, and multi-site users may repeat the flow per site (documented limitation).
blockers.howToClear: Build the accessible-resources lookup and cloudid-scoped URL construction into your client from day one; prefer account-level grants for multi-site products.
blockers.title: Site-scoped (cloudid) plumbing

blockers.detail: Changing scopes later forces every previously consented user to re-consent to the new set. A new consent overrides the previous grant's scopes entirely.
blockers.howToClear: Finalize your scope list before enabling sharing; batch any changes.
blockers.title: Scope changes force re-consent

alternatives: Forge apps (Atlassian-hosted platform with manifest scopes; a different product model, not a standalone external integration)
Connect apps (developer-hosted, JWT app descriptor; 3LO is not supported for Connect apps)
flavor.recommended: OAuth 2.0 (3LO) app in the Atlassian developer console
flavor.why: 3LO (three-legged OAuth) is the standalone external integration: nothing installs into the customer's site UI, users authorize via a consent link, and your backend calls api.atlassian.com. At creation you choose the grant type: account-level (one consent can cover multiple sites) vs resource-level (consent limited to the sites the user selects). Pick account-level for multi-site agent products.

humanMust: Log in with your Atlassian account and create the app
Choose the grant type and the scope set (product decisions)
Copy and vault the client secret
Provide a test instance if you pursue Marketplace approval
name: Jira (Atlassian)
nuances: Scopes come in two families: classic (broad, e.g. read:jira-work; recommended where available) and granular (fine-grained per resource). Jira Software supports granular only, so a multi-product app may mix both; one classic scope can map to roughly nine granular ones.
Regardless of scopes, the app can never do more than the authorizing user themselves can do in Jira.
The implicit grant flow is not supported for 3LO, a constraint for pure client-side apps.

Atlassian's security guidance says collecting API tokens from customers or telling each customer to create their own 3LO app violates its cloud-app security requirements; the compliant pattern is one distributable 3LO app per integration.
Admins cannot revoke a single user's grant from the Connected Apps screen; the grant lives between user and app, and only uninstalling the app cuts it off.
prerequisites: The APIs (Jira, Confluence, User Identity) and scope set your agent needs
offline_access in your scope list if you need refresh tokens (you do)

steps.detail: developer.atlassian.com/console > Create > OAuth 2.0 integration: name the app and choose the grant type (account-level vs resource-level). The app is private by default.
steps.title: Create the 3LO app

steps.detail: Permissions (left menu) > Add each API you need (Jira API, Confluence API, User Identity API) > Configure > add classic and/or granular scopes. Note Jira Software exposes granular scopes only. Always include offline_access if you need refresh tokens.
steps.title: Add APIs and scopes

steps.detail: Authorization > OAuth 2.0 (3LO) > Configure: enter the Callback URL and Save. The redirect_uri sent at runtime must match it exactly.
steps.title: Set the callback URL

steps.detail: Settings shows the Client ID and Secret (your client_id/client_secret), plus name/description/avatar. Vault the secret.
steps.title: Copy the client ID and secret

steps.detail: Send users to auth.atlassian.com/authorize (audience=api.atlassian.com, client_id, scope, redirect_uri, state, response_type=code, prompt=consent); exchange the code at auth.atlassian.com/oauth/token; then GET api.atlassian.com/oauth/token/accessible-resources to learn the user's sites and cloudids; call product APIs at api.atlassian.com/ex/jira/{cloudid}/... with the bearer token. Note: requests go via api.atlassian.com, not the customer's atlassian.net domain.
steps.title: Implement the flow (with cloudid discovery)

steps.detail: Distribution (left menu) > toggle Enable sharing, then send users the Authorization URL from the 3LO configuration. No queue, no cap stated. Users will see a warning that the integration has not been reviewed by Atlassian until you complete the optional step below.
steps.title: Enable sharing

steps.detail: (Optional, to remove the unreviewed warning) Submit via the Marketplace 'Publish a new app' flow as a third-party integration ('My app isn't directly installable'), with an informational listing and access to a test instance of your software for the reviewer. General listing guidance: expect first contact within 5-10 business days.
steps.time: Packet prep ~half a day; first response stated at 5-10 business days
steps.title: (Optional) Get Marketplace approval

tagline: No approval stands between you and your users: flip on sharing and anyone can connect today. The only price is a warning banner ('not yet reviewed by Atlassian') until you pass an optional Marketplace review.

time.active: ~30 min of console work + ~2-3 hrs of flow code (cloudid plumbing included)
time.total: Same day to users connecting; optional warning removal adds a review cycle
time.waiting: None for sharing; 5-10 business days to first response for optional Marketplace approval (general listing guidance)
